2027-04-28.title: Wednesday of the Fifth Week of Easter · St Peter Chanel; St Louis Grignion de Montfort
readings: They went up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders to discuss this question
Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit
2027-04-28.alt: Easter weekday of the fifth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the Paschal candle stays lit beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorials: St Peter Chanel, priest and martyr (colour red if his Mass is said), and St Louis Grignion de Montfort, priest (white). The Gospel of the vine was also read on Sunday; on this weekday it is heard beside the first great dispute of the Church.
2027-04-28.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
theo: The door of faith has been opened to the Gentiles, and with that joy comes the Church's first great argument. “Certain individuals came down from Judea” to Antioch and taught: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” These were believers in Jesus; the question was real. Must a Gentile first become a Jew in order to become a Christian? Luke does not hide that there was “no small dissension and debate.” What matters is what the Church did next. No one walked out to found a rival church. Paul and Barnabas “and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to discuss this question with the apostles and the elders.” On the way, through Phoenicia and Samaria, they told of the conversion of the Gentiles “and brought great joy to all the believers.” In Jerusalem they are welcomed by “the church and the apostles and the elders,” some believers from the party of the Pharisees state their view, and “The apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter.” This is the Council of Jerusalem, about the year 49, the pattern for every council since: when the faith is disputed, the Church gathers around the apostles and their successors and waits on the Holy Spirit. The Psalm sings of the city where the tribes go up together: “Jerusalem, built as a city that is bound firmly together.”

The Gospel of the true vine, heard on Sunday, now sounds beside this first dispute. “I am the vine, you are the branches.” Branches do not choose one another; they are joined because each one is joined to the vine. The unity the apostles seek in Jerusalem is not a committee's agreement but life flowing from Christ into every member. Jesus also speaks of a painful grace: “Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.” Anyone who has seen a vine cut back in winter knows that pruning looks like loss. Today the Church remembers two priests who were pruned to the root. St Peter Chanel (1803 to 1841), a French priest of the Society of Mary, laboured for over three years on the Pacific island of Futuna with few visible results, and was clubbed to death on 28 April 1841; within a few years almost the whole island had asked for baptism, and he is honoured as the first martyr of Oceania. St Louis Grignion de Montfort (1673 to 1716) preached missions across western France, often rejected and even banned from dioceses, and wrote of total consecration to Jesus through the hands of the Blessed Virgin Mary; his little book, found long after his death, gave St John Paul II his motto, Totus tuus. Both stayed on the vine, and the fruit came after them.
outline: Ask: when Christians disagree, what do we usually do?
A real question in the young Church.
Point 2 · They went up to Jerusalem
Disputes brought to the apostles, not to the street.
Point 3 · Pruned to bear more fruit
Abiding in the vine; St Peter Chanel and St Louis de Montfort.
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
live: If you are in a dispute in your family, parish or work, seek a calm conversation with the right person instead of complaining to others.
Name one loss or disappointment of this year and offer it to the Father in prayer as pruning for more fruit.
2027-04-28.prayer: Father, you are the vinegrower and your Son is the true vine. Keep us joined to him and to one another, so that, when we disagree, we may seek the truth together in the communion of your Church, as the apostles did in Jerusalem. Prune us where we need it and make us bear fruit that lasts. Through the prayers of St Peter Chanel, who gave his life on Futuna, and of St Louis Grignion de Montfort, who gave himself wholly to Jesus through Mary, make us faithful branches. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The vine gives its wine, and the wine becomes his Blood. At every Mass the sap of the true Vine flows into the branches: in the Eucharist we, many as we are, become one body, because we all share the one bread and the one cup.

quick: In Antioch some believers taught that Gentile converts must be circumcised to be saved, and a sharp debate began.
Instead of dividing, the Church sent Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders, who met to consider the question.
Jesus is the vine and we are the branches; the Father prunes us so that we bear more fruit. St Peter Chanel and St Louis de Montfort bore fruit after their deaths.
2027-04-28.action: Pray today for unity among Christians, and for one person you disagree with.
2027-04-28.question: When I disagree with someone in the Church, do I seek communion or do I walk away?
kidsaint: A French priest who sailed across the ocean to a tiny island called Futuna. He learned the people's language and looked after the sick so kindly that they called him the man with the good heart. Some people did not want him there, and he was killed. Soon afterwards almost everyone on the island became a Christian. Lesson: love is never wasted, even when we cannot see the fruit yet.

family.explain: Long ago the first Christians had a big argument. They did not split up. They went to Jerusalem to ask the apostles, Peter and the others, and they prayed and talked it through together. Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches. A branch that stays on the plant has fruit; a branch that falls off dries up.
family.intention: We pray for Christians in Oceania and the Pacific islands, through St Peter Chanel, and for families where there are quarrels.
family.ask: Ask: “When we argue at home, how can we solve it like the first Christians did?”

illus: St Peter Chanel arrived on the small Pacific island of Futuna in 1837. He learned the language, cared for the sick, and was called by the islanders the man with the good heart, yet in more than three years only a handful asked for baptism. When the son of the island's ruler wished to become a Christian, the ruler's anger turned on the missionary, and on 28 April 1841 Peter was clubbed to death. Within a few years almost the whole island had become Catholic. The pruning had been severe; the fruit came after him.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, true vine, keep us joined to you and to one another. Amen.
share: After Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them (Acts 15:2). How do I behave in a disagreement?
They reported the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the believers (Acts 15:3). Do I rejoice when others come to faith, even if they are different from me?
Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit (John 15:2). What pruning is God doing in my life?
pm.resp: Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord.
interc: For the unity of the Church, and for all Christian communities divided by disputes.
For the Pope and the bishops, successors of the apostles, that the Spirit may guide their decisions.
For the Church in Oceania and for missionaries in difficult places, through St Peter Chanel.
For all who consecrate themselves to Jesus through Mary, through St Louis de Montfort.
For our group, that we may abide in Christ and bear fruit that lasts.
pm.close: Father, you prune the branches so that they may bear more fruit. Keep us in your Son and in the communion of his Church. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the young Church had hardly begun when it faced a serious question. Some believers came to Antioch and taught: unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved (Acts 15:1). Paul and Barnabas disagreed strongly. Luke says honestly: there was no small dissension and debate.

What did they do? Nobody started a new church. They went up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders, and on the way they told of the Gentiles' conversion and brought great joy to all the believers. In Jerusalem the apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter (Acts 15:6). When Christians disagree, the way of the Church is not to split, but to gather with the successors of the apostles and listen to the Holy Spirit.

Jesus tells us why this matters: I am the vine, you are the branches. Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Branches are united because each one draws life from the same vine. And the vinegrower prunes every fruitful branch to make it bear more. Pruning hurts. It looks like loss. But it is the Father's care.

St Peter Chanel worked for years on a Pacific island with little fruit and was killed there; soon the whole island believed. St Louis de Montfort was rejected again and again, and his writing on giving oneself to Jesus through Mary bore fruit long after his death. Let us stay on the vine, accept the pruning, and trust the Father with the fruit. Amen.
kids: Children, have you seen a grape vine or a pepper vine climbing a tree? The leaves and fruit grow only on branches that stay joined to the plant. Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches. When we pray, go to Mass and love one another, we stay joined to Jesus. St Peter Chanel went to a faraway island to tell people about Jesus. He was killed there, but later everyone on the island came to love Jesus. His love bore fruit!

intro: Theme: “Apart from me you can do nothing.”
The first dispute of the Church brought to the apostles, the branches joined to the vine, and the Father's pruning; St Peter Chanel and St Louis Grignion de Montfort.

sub: Must a Gentile first become a Jew?
q: How very good and pleasant it is when kindred live together in unity!
making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
points.apply: In your next disagreement, listen fully to the other person before you answer.

sub: Not a split but a journey.
q: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the Lord!”
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;
points.apply: Pray this week for the Pope and your bishop, and read one short teaching of the Church on a question that troubles you.

sub: Fruit after death: Peter Chanel and Montfort.
q: Blessed are those who trust in the Lord, whose trust is the Lord. They shall be like a tree planted by water, sending out its roots by the stream.
Now, discipline always seems painful rather than pleasant at the time, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
points.apply: Offer one present pain to the Father as pruning, and ask for the fruit he wants, not the fruit you want.

concl: The first Christians met disagreement by going to the apostles and waiting on the Spirit.
The branches stay one by staying on the vine; the Father's pruning, as the saints of today show, brings fruit that outlives us.
2027-04-28.resolve: Make one step of reconciliation this week, and offer one pain to the Father.
